bodyChanges: They may start noticing the first signs of pregnancy this week — things like breast tenderness, headaches, lower backaches, and nausea.
babySize: Their baby is incredibly tiny right now, measuring about 0.078 inches (roughly 2 millimeters) in length.
babyDevelopment: Their baby now has three distinct layers — the ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm — each of which will develop into different organs and tissues.
funFact: Breast tenderness and soreness are usually the first cues that pregnancy has begun, caused by rising hormones.

bodyChanges: Changes may not be visible to others yet, but they might start feeling more pregnancy symptoms this week, including morning sickness — which affects around half of all pregnant people.
babySize: Their baby measures about 0.118 inches (3 millimeters) long, measured from crown to rump (CRL).
babyDevelopment: Their baby looks a bit like a tiny tadpole at this stage. The heart is already beating steadily, and the structures that will become the eyes and ears are starting to take shape. The fetal skeleton is also beginning to form.

bodyChanges: They might have gained a few pounds by now, though some people lose a little weight early on. Breast tenderness and darkening areolas are common, and heartburn may appear. Some light spotting with mild cramping can happen and is usually normal, though heavy bleeding or worsening cramps should be checked out.
babySize: Their baby is about ¾ of an inch (19 millimeters) long.
babyDevelopment: Growth is moving fast this week. The neural tube — which will become the brain and spinal cord — is closing along the baby's back. The heart is forming and already beating. The lungs, jaw, nose, and palate are developing, and tiny hand and foot buds have webbed structures that will eventually become fingers and toes. A vaginal ultrasound may even pick up a heartbeat.
funFact: Their baby's tiny heart has started beating. They might also notice a sudden, heightened sense of smell — completely normal at this stage.

bodyChanges: Their body is changing gradually, though it probably isn't obvious to those around them yet. They may have gained a couple of pounds — or lost a little if morning sickness has been rough.
babySize: Their baby is about an inch (2.54 centimeters) long by the end of this week and weighs less than an aspirin.
babyDevelopment: Every essential organ has begun forming in the embryo's tiny body. Hair and nipple follicles are taking shape, and the eyelids and tongue have started developing.

bodyChanges: Things may look the same on the outside, but a lot is happening internally. Before pregnancy the uterus was about the size of a fist — it's now closer to the size of a grapefruit. Breast tenderness is common as the body prepares for lactation, and blood volume is increasing significantly.
babySize: Their baby is just over an inch (about 2.54 centimeters) long — roughly the size of a bean.
babyDevelopment: Everything present in an adult human is now present in the baby in some form. The ears continue developing inside and out. Bones are beginning to form and muscles can already contract. Fingers and toes are lengthening, facial features are maturing, and the embryonic tail is disappearing as the body straightens out. The baby's sex has already been determined genetically, though external genitals are still forming.
funFact: First-trimester fatigue is real! Their baby is growing rapidly, and webbed fingers and toes are already sprouting.

bodyChanges: They might not look pregnant to others yet, but they're definitely starting to notice changes themselves. Mood swings, heartburn, and feeling more bloated are all common this week.
babySize: Their baby is about the size of a grape — measuring around 1.67 inches (4.24 centimeters) from head to rump and weighing just a fraction of an ounce.
babyDevelopment: Though still tiny, their baby is gearing up for rapid weight gain. They're also starting to look much more like a little person — the embryonic tail has completely disappeared by week 9.

bodyChanges: The uterus has continued growing, but there may not be much of a visible bump yet. Some people feel ready to share their news at this point, while others are still getting used to the idea.
babySize: Their baby is a little over 2 inches (5 centimeters) long — about the size of a lime — and weighs around a quarter of an ounce (7 grams).
babyDevelopment: This marks the end of the embryonic period and the beginning of the fetal period. The major vital organs — including the kidneys, liver, brain, and lungs — are now functioning, and will continue to mature throughout the rest of the pregnancy.

bodyChanges: Some people notice changes in their hair, fingernails, and toenails this week — things like faster growth. These changes are completely normal during pregnancy.
babySize: Their baby is over 2½ inches (6.35 centimeters) long from crown to rump and weighs about half an ounce (14 grams).
babyDevelopment: Their baby's head still makes up nearly half of their total length. By week 11, the fingers and toes have fully separated. The skin is still very transparent, and the bones are starting to harden.

bodyChanges: The uterus is growing enough that a healthcare provider can now feel it in the lower abdomen. Maternity clothes may start feeling necessary, especially for those who've been pregnant before. Skin changes like darkening areolas and irregular patches called chloasma (the 'mask of pregnancy') can appear, though these typically fade after delivery.
babySize: Their baby is about 3.15 inches (8 centimeters) long and weighs around 1 ounce (28 grams) by the end of this week.
babyDevelopment: The baby is taking on a more recognizable look — the eyes are moving closer together and the ears are nearing their final position. The intestines, which have been in the umbilical cord, are beginning to move into the abdomen. The kidneys can now produce urine, the nervous system continues maturing, and the baby may even start developing reflexes like sucking.
funFact: Their baby is making amazing movements — curling tiny toes, opening and closing their hands, and even making sucking motions.

bodyChanges: Tighter clothes are probably being swapped for something more comfortable. Morning sickness may start to ease up this week, though heartburn can become more frequent. Breasts continue changing as they prepare for lactation — they may feel larger or lumpy, with veins becoming more visible. Colostrum, the first stage of breast milk, begins forming during the second trimester.
babySize: By week 13, their baby is almost 3¾ inches (9.5 centimeters) long and weighs about 1¼ ounces (35 grams).
babyDevelopment: Their baby's head is now about one-third of their body length — much more proportional! Unique fingerprints are forming at the fingertips. The kidneys and urinary tract are fully functional, and a fine, soft hair called lanugo is beginning to develop over their skin.

bodyChanges: Maternity clothes may be a necessity for some people at this point, while others make do with creative solutions like rubber bands to expand waistbands.
babySize: Their baby is now over 4 inches (10 centimeters) long and weighs just under 2 ounces.
babyDevelopment: Their baby's arms are lengthening and becoming more proportional to the rest of the body. The liver is beginning to produce bile, and the spleen is starting to produce red blood cells.
funFact: Their baby is now making tiny expressions with their developing facial features.

bodyChanges: Average weight gain at this point is around 5 pounds (2.27 kilograms). The top of the uterus can be felt about four to five inches below the belly button. First trimester symptoms may be improving, though some people still experience nausea. Body aches, tingling in the hands and feet, nosebleeds, and sensitive gums can also occur.
babySize: By the end of this week, their baby is about 4¾ inches (12 centimeters) long and weighs around 2 ounces (57 grams).
babyDevelopment: The skin is still very thin with visible blood vessels beneath it. The ears are continuing to develop and look more recognizable, and the eyes are repositioning toward the center of the face. The bones are beginning to ossify — meaning a skeleton would now show up on an x-ray. Babies are often seen sucking their thumbs on ultrasound at this stage.

bodyChanges: The uterus weighs about 8½ ounces and keeps growing. The placenta is expanding and amniotic fluid is increasing around the baby. Blood volume rises by 30–50%, which can give a noticeable glow to the face — thanks to hormonal changes stimulating oil glands.
babySize: Their baby is approximately 5.31 inches (13.5 centimeters) long from crown to rump and weighs about 2½ ounces.
babyDevelopment: The head is becoming more upright, and the ears and eyes are now settled into their final positions. The circulatory system is working hard — the baby's heart is already pumping around 25 quarts of blood per day, a number that will rise to about 1,900 quarts per day by week 40.

bodyChanges: As the abdomen continues to grow, other organs shift to make room for the expanding uterus and baby.
babySize: Their baby is a little over 5¾ inches (14.5 centimeters) long and weighs about 4 ounces.
babyDevelopment: The umbilical cord is getting longer, thicker, and stronger for the weeks ahead. The ears have fully formed and moved into their final position, so the baby can now begin to hear. Fat tissue is also starting to develop, which will help fill out their features and regulate temperature and metabolism.

bodyChanges: The belly is now visibly changing, and most people can tell a pregnancy is underway. Cardiovascular changes may cause some dizziness from low blood pressure, so it's helpful to move slowly when getting up from lying or sitting.
babySize: Their baby is about 6.29 inches (16 centimeters) long and weighs around 5½ ounces.
babyDevelopment: A protective covering called myelin is starting to form around the baby's nerves. In female fetuses, the fallopian tubes and uterus are moving into their proper positions. In male fetuses, the genitals may be visible on ultrasound — though not always at this stage.

bodyChanges: Round ligament pain is a common companion in the second trimester — a sharp pain in the abdomen or hip area on one or both sides as the round ligament stretches to support the growing uterus.
babySize: Their baby is just under 7 inches (17.8 centimeters) long and weighs about 7 ounces.
babyDevelopment: The kidneys are producing urine, and hair is beginning to sprout on the baby's scalp. The parts of the brain responsible for the senses are also specializing. In female fetuses, around 6 million eggs have already formed in the ovaries.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now at the same level as the belly button — the halfway point! Weight gain of around 8 to 10 pounds is typical by now, with roughly half a pound to a pound expected each week for the rest of the pregnancy.
babySize: Their baby is about 7¾ inches (19.7 centimeters) long and weighs approximately 9 ounces.
babyDevelopment: Their baby is now covered in a white, waxy coating called vernix caseosa, which protects their skin from the amniotic fluid. They're also beginning to produce meconium — the dark substance that will be their first bowel movement after birth.
funFact: Estrogen levels are prolonging the hair's growth phase — meaning they'll lose less hair than usual and nails may grow faster too.

bodyChanges: The vast majority of people they encounter will now be able to tell they're expecting. The uterus can be felt just above the belly button. Some swelling in the feet and ankles toward the end of the day is common.
babySize: Their baby has grown to over 8½ inches (21.6 centimeters) long — now measured crown to heel — and weighs about 12 ounces.
babyDevelopment: The baby's eyelids have finished forming this week. They're very active, moving around and swallowing amniotic fluid, which is helping their digestive system mature. In female fetuses, the vagina continues to develop.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now about ¾ of an inch (2 centimeters) above the belly button. Many people describe the second trimester as the most comfortable stretch of pregnancy.
babySize: Their baby is almost 10 inches (25 centimeters) long and weighs a full 14 ounces.
babyDevelopment: Their baby is starting to look like a newborn — just much smaller. The skin still appears wrinkly because they haven't yet gained enough weight to fill it out. The lips are becoming more distinct, the eyes are fully formed (though the iris still lacks pigment), and the pancreas is continuing to mature.

bodyChanges: The uterus now extends about 1½ inches (3.8 centimeters) above the belly button. Weight gain of around 12 to 15 pounds is typical by this point. The uterus pressing on the bladder may cause some leakage — if fluid seems different from urine (amniotic fluid is odorless), it's worth checking in with a healthcare provider.
babySize: Their baby has reached 1 pound (0.45 kilograms) and is approximately 11 to 14 inches (28 to 36 centimeters) long.
babyDevelopment: Their baby is filling out and starting to look more and more like a newborn. The fine body hair (lanugo) may be darkening, and is sometimes visible on ultrasound.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now about 2 inches (5 centimeters) above the belly button. The skin on the abdomen and breasts is stretching, which can cause itchiness — a good moisturizer can help. Eyes may also feel drier than usual.
babySize: Their baby is over 12½ inches (32 centimeters) long and weighs between 1¼ and 1½ pounds.
babyDevelopment: The baby's brain is growing rapidly this week. Taste buds are forming, and the lungs are becoming more developed and complex — including the cells that produce surfactant, which will be crucial for breathing after birth.
funFact: The top of the uterus has risen above the belly button and is now about the size of a soccer ball!

bodyChanges: The uterus is now about the size of a soccer ball, with its top felt roughly halfway between the belly button and the bottom of the sternum.
babySize: Their baby is about 13 inches (33 centimeters) long and weighs between 1½ and 1¾ pounds.
babyDevelopment: Their baby is slowly gaining baby fat, which will help fill out their skin and make them appear less wrinkly. If they have hair, its color and texture might even be visible on ultrasound.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now about 2½ inches (6.3 centimeters) above the belly button, growing roughly half an inch per week from here on. Weight gain of about 16 to 22 pounds is typical by this point.
babySize: Their baby is approximately 13.38 inches (34 centimeters) long and weighs about 2 pounds.
babyDevelopment: Auditory nerves are developing, allowing the baby to respond more reliably to sounds. They continue swallowing amniotic fluid, which supports lung development. In male fetuses, the testicles have begun their descent into the scrotum.

bodyChanges: Baby's movements are much more noticeable now — some feel like hiccups, others like a full aerobic workout in there! If movement seems to slow down significantly, it's worth mentioning to a healthcare provider.
babySize: Their baby is now 13¾ inches (35 centimeters) long and weighs about 2¼ pounds (1 kilogram).
babyDevelopment: Around weeks 27 to 28, the baby can open and close their eyes for the first time. They've established regular sleep-wake cycles — though not necessarily in sync with anyone else's! Those rhythmic fluttery movements? Probably hiccups, which are very common as the lungs continue to develop.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now well above the belly button — about 3½ inches (8.9 centimeters) or more. Weight gain of 17 to 24 pounds is typical by now. As the third trimester gets underway, leg cramps, constipation, insomnia, and hemorrhoids become more common.
babySize: Their baby is about 14¼ inches (36 centimeters) long and weighs around 2½ pounds (1.13 kilograms) — with significant weight gain still ahead.
babyDevelopment: The brain is becoming more sophisticated, developing grooves and folds on its surface. Eyebrows and eyelashes are now visible, scalp hair is growing longer, and fat storage under the skin continues to develop, giving the baby a rounder appearance.

bodyChanges: Total weight gain of 19 to 25 pounds is typical by now. The top of the uterus can be felt 3½ to 4 inches above the belly button.
babySize: Their baby now measures over 14½ inches (37 centimeters) and weighs about 2¾ pounds (1.25 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby is growing rapidly — their head is getting bigger as brain development continues to accelerate. Muscles and lungs are also maturing. With so much happening, it's an especially good time to make sure nutrition is solid: protein, vitamin C, folic acid, iron, and calcium are all important right now.

bodyChanges: Tiredness is more pronounced now, and getting comfortable enough to sleep can be a challenge. Mood swings are common in the third trimester. Hormonal changes can also loosen joints — some people even find their shoe size changes permanently.
babySize: Their baby is about 15.15 inches (38.5 centimeters) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby's eyes are becoming more mature — they can now distinguish between light and darkness and follow light sources. After birth, newborn vision is typically around 20/400, gradually improving over time.

bodyChanges: Colostrum — a thick, yellowish pre-milk — may begin leaking from the breasts. Nursing pads can help with that. Braxton Hicks contractions may also become more noticeable: practice contractions lasting 30 seconds to 2 minutes that help the body prepare for labor.
babySize: Their baby is over 15½ inches (39.4 centimeters) long and weighs between 3½ and 4 pounds (1.6 to 1.8 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby can now turn their head from side to side and is moving so much it might make sleeping a challenge! All that activity is a great sign. They're continuing to build fat under their skin, giving them more and more of a newborn look.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now about 5 inches above the belly button — so high it may press on the diaphragm, causing shortness of breath and heartburn. Weight gain continues at about a pound a week, and blood volume has increased by 40–50% over the course of the pregnancy.
babySize: Their baby is a little over 16 inches (40.6 centimeters) long and weighs between 4 and 4½ pounds (1.8 to 2 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Toenails and fingernails have fully formed. The lungs are continuing to mature, though they won't be fully developed for a few more weeks. The skeleton is complete, but the bones are still soft and pliable.
funFact: Their baby will gain a third to half of their birth weight in the next seven weeks as they prepare for the outside world.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now a little over 5 inches (12.7 centimeters) from the belly button. Total weight gain of 22 to 28 pounds is typical by now. Only about 1 in 10 people experience a dramatic gush when their water breaks — many notice a slow leak instead. Amniotic fluid is clear and odorless; if there's any uncertainty, it's worth calling a healthcare provider.
babySize: Their baby is approximately 16½ inches (42 centimeters) long and weighs between 4½ and 5 pounds (2 to 2.3 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby's skin is becoming less red and wrinkled as fat stores continue to build up. The bones are hardening — with the important exception of the skull, which stays soft and flexible to help with delivery.
funFact: The bones in their baby's skull are not fused together yet, which allows their head to shift and squeeze through the birth canal.

bodyChanges: The top of the uterus is now about 5½ inches (14 centimeters) above the belly button. Amniotic fluid is at its peak around this time and will begin to decrease after week 37. Some people notice their belly button has popped out or become more sensitive.
babySize: Their baby is around 17½ inches (44.5 centimeters) long and weighs about 5 to 5½ pounds (2.3 to 2.5 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Fat is continuing to build up under the skin — important for temperature regulation after birth. The central nervous system keeps maturing, and the lungs are now well-developed. At this stage, babies have good survival chances outside the womb, though staying in until 38–40 weeks is still the goal.

bodyChanges: There are about 6 inches (15.2 centimeters) from the belly button to the top of the uterus. Total weight gain of 24 to 29 pounds is typical. As the baby 'drops' into the pelvis (called lightening), breathing gets a little easier — though the bladder feels more pressure.
babySize: Their baby is between 17 and 18 inches (43.2 to 45.7 centimeters) long and weighs about 5½ to 6 pounds (2.5 to 2.7 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: The vast majority of their baby's growth is complete. The kidneys are fully developed, and the liver is beginning to process waste. Movement may feel a bit different now as space gets tighter, but the frequency should stay the same.

bodyChanges: Their baby is gaining about an ounce a day, though overall weight gain may level off. The body may feel stretched and fatigued. Braxton Hicks contractions often increase — actual labor contractions will be more intense and regular.
babySize: Their baby is likely between 17½ and 19 inches (44.5 to 48.3 centimeters) long and weighs 5¾ to 6¾ pounds (2.6 to 3.1 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: The downy lanugo hair and the waxy vernix caseosa that's been protecting the baby's skin are beginning to disappear. The baby has typically settled into a head-down position by now; if not, a healthcare provider can discuss options.

bodyChanges: Weight gain may level off from here, with a total of 25 to 35 pounds being typical. Amniotic fluid is decreasing and Braxton Hicks contractions are more frequent. The cervix is beginning to dilate and efface. They may also pass the mucus plug — a sign the cervix is opening. Labor could still be hours, days, or even weeks away.
babySize: Their baby is about 18 inches (45.7 centimeters) long and weighs between 6 and 7 pounds (2.7 to 3.2 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby is considered full-term after week 37, though staying in the womb until fully ready is still ideal. If the baby isn't in a head-down position, it's worth talking with the healthcare provider about options.

bodyChanges: Some swelling in the feet is normal at this stage. However, sudden or severe swelling in the hands, face, feet, or ankles should be reported to a healthcare provider right away — it can sometimes signal pregnancy-induced hypertension or preeclampsia.
babySize: Their baby is probably between 17 and 20 inches (43.2 to 50.8 centimeters) long and weighs about 6¼ to 7½ pounds (2.8 to 3.4 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Almost all of the baby's organs are mature and fully functioning. The brain and lungs can function outside the womb, though they'll continue maturing well into childhood. Eye color at birth may change in the weeks and months after delivery.

bodyChanges: The cervix is effacing — softening, shortening, and thinning as the baby descends into the birth canal. This is the body's natural preparation for labor.
babySize: Their baby is between 18 and 20½ inches (45.7 to 52 centimeters) long and weighs about 6½ to 8 pounds (2.9 to 3.6 kilograms).
babyDevelopment: Their baby is still building fat beneath the skin to help regulate their body temperature after birth. They're also shedding older skin cells and replacing them with fresh new ones.

bodyChanges: When labor begins and pushing starts, the baby's head will appear with each contraction — a moment called crowning. As the baby's head stretches the vaginal opening, there's often an intense burning sensation known as 'the ring of fire,' followed by a natural numbness as the tissue stretches thin.
babySize: Their baby should be between 19 and 21 inches (48.3 to 53.3 centimeters) long and weigh anywhere from 6¾ to 10 pounds.
babyDevelopment: The baby's bones have hardened everywhere except the skull, which stays soft and flexible for delivery. The skull plates can even overlap slightly, which is why some newborns have a temporarily cone-shaped head — it rounds out quickly! Babies are born with two soft spots (fontanelles): the back one closes at 3–4 months, the front by 8–15 months.
funFact: Babies rarely arrive exactly on their due date — only about 5% make their debut right on schedule!
